title: Checkpoint: the developer as a control system
summary: Phase 1 taught eight subjects that look separate: the job, judgment, deal psychology, physiology, communication, wealth and protection. This checkpoint lesson shows they are one system with one purpose, protecting a thin residual from bad decisions, and revisits the hardest idea from each week.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a developer is paid last, from a thin residual, so everything in Phase 1 comes down to one job: keep bad decisions away from that residual. Judgment, psychology, your body, your words, your balance sheet and your protections are all parts of the same control system.

Recall

Q. What generally makes a will valid, in concept?

A. It must meet the formal requirements of the law that applies, such as being in writing, signed and properly witnessed, and the person making it must have the mental capacity to do so; verify the requirements with an estate lawyer where you live.

Q. What is a liquidity floor?

A. A set amount of cash or near-cash, held outside your deals, that covers essential spending for a chosen number of months and is never used for a deal.

Q. Why is a developer's profit called a residual?

A. Because it is what is left after every fixed claim, from the lender to the contractor, has been paid, so a small change in value or cost becomes a large change in profit.

Why this matters

This is a checkpoint week. Each teacher revisits the hardest idea of Phase 1 from their own seat, and the week ends with a mock interview and a recording you score yourself. The danger at a checkpoint is to treat it as a list of topics to tick off. The goal is the opposite: to see that eight weeks taught one discipline. When you can explain that discipline in three minutes to a lender or a partner, you will sound like a developer who has thought about how he decides, which is rarer than one who knows the vocabulary.

The thin residual, again

Plain English: you get what is left. In Week 1, a hypothetical 60-unit building cost 14 million dollars and was worth 16 million, a profit of 2 million. Rents 5 percent low cut that profit by 40 percent. A 10 percent cost overrun cut it by 70 percent. Nobody else at the table lost anything like that.

The professional framing is leverage inside the residual: a small percentage change in either of two large numbers becomes a large percentage change in their difference. Every week since has been a defence of that difference. The gate protects it from momentum. The outside view protects it from optimism. Incentive analysis protects it from advisers' interests. The red window protects it from your own fatigue. Clear writing protects it from misunderstanding. The liquidity floor protects you when it turns negative anyway.

Four failure modes, four controls

Plain English: Phase 1 named four ways good people make bad calls, and gave each a control that is written down rather than felt.

First, the decision is made on hope instead of evidence. The control is the outside view and Rule 2: write the reference-class figure beside your own and explain the gap. Second, the decision is pushed by people or forces with their own interests: the seller's anchor, the consultant's fee, a sunk cost, the wish to avoid a loss. The control is to ask how each person is paid and to decide from today forward. Third, the decision is made by a tired or stressed brain. The control is Rule 4 and the red window. Fourth, the decision is made on a message that hid the risk or a word that bound you without meaning to. The control is Rules 5 and 6: risk in the first line, and changes to load or life safety approved only in writing with the check behind them.

Worked example one. A hypothetical Thursday. At 05:30, after a night shift, a seller texts that another buyer has offered more and asks you to confirm today at 1,200,000 dollars, 100,000 above your written walk-away price. Run the system. The fatigue control comes first: you are in your red window, so the only reply is a holding answer, "I'll respond by 14:00." Then the interests control: the other buyer may be real or may be an anchor, and the seller is paid more if you believe it. Then the evidence control: your walk-away price came from comparable sales, and nothing in the text changes that evidence. Last, the words control: by 14:00, rested, you reply in writing, bottom line first, with nothing in it that could be read as accepting a higher price: "My offer stands at 1,100,000 dollars, conditional on the soil study. I understand if you take the other offer." That single morning used five weeks of Phase 1. Notice what the system did not do. It did not decide whether to buy. It made sure the decision was made by a rested person, on evidence, with words that said exactly what he meant.

Say that out loud now.

Say it this way: hope, interests, fatigue, words; outside view, incentives, red window, writing.

The personal half of the system

Weeks 7 and 8 moved the same logic from the project to you. A project can fail without destroying you only if your balance sheet was built for it. That means a liquidity floor no deal can touch, concentration you have measured rather than assumed, personal guarantees you understand, and Rule 7: size every commitment so its worst case leaves the floor untouched. And it means Rule 8: a will and powers of attorney signed before the first personal guarantee, because a project that loses its decision-maker without a plan can lose its lender too.

Worked example two. Suppose, hypothetically, you have 600,000 dollars of liquid savings and a liquidity floor of 150,000 dollars. A deal needs 300,000 dollars of your equity and a personal guarantee capped at 400,000 dollars. Worst case: the equity is lost and the guarantee is called in full, 700,000 dollars in total. That exceeds your 600,000 dollars of liquidity, so the floor does not survive. Rule 7 says you do not sign as structured. Options include a smaller guarantee, a partner sharing it, or a smaller share of the deal. The deal may be excellent. The structure is not survivable.

How the best do it

Large developers and contractors run formal investment committees and stage-gate reviews, in which a project cannot draw its next tranche of money without a written paper, an independent challenge and a recorded decision. Many also keep strict limits on how much of the firm any single project can put at risk. A one-person developer can copy all of it: a one-page memo for every gate, one trusted person who argues the other side, a decision journal, and a written limit on what any one deal may put at stake.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is knowing the controls and not using them when it counts, because under time pressure each one feels like a delay. The control is to make them automatic: the red window as a rule on your phone, the memo template as the only way a decision reaches you, and the liquidity floor in a separate account.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats the soft weeks, psychology, sleep and communication, as optional extras to the hard weeks of numbers to come. Phase 1's failure cases say otherwise. Columbia, the Hyatt Regency walkways and the Exxon Valdez were not caused by bad arithmetic.

Callback

In Week 2 you started a decision journal. Read your entries from the last seven weeks today. Look for the pattern: were your weakest calls made tired, rushed, under someone else's anchor, or on a message you did not fully read? That pattern is your personal reference class, and it tells you which control you need most.

Recap

Phase 1 is one system protecting a thin residual. Four failure modes, hope, interests, fatigue and words, each have a written control. The personal half, liquidity, concentration, guarantees and protection, makes sure a failed deal does not become a failed life. This week tests whether you can use the system, not just describe it.

Next: Ford, Failure Forensics, on a composite case: a handshake partnership that broke when the land became valuable.
checklist: Read your decision journal from the last seven weeks and name your most common failure mode.
Write your four controls on one card: outside view, incentives, red window, writing.
Set your red window as a recurring rule on your phone.
Make the one-page memo the only way a decision reaches you.
Hold your liquidity floor in a separate account no deal can draw on.
Test your next commitment against Rule 7: does its worst case leave the floor untouched?
Name one person who will argue the other side of your next gate decision.
head: Field checklist
speak: A developer is paid last, from a thin residual. In a hypothetical building costing 14 million and worth 16, a 10 percent overrun takes 70 percent of the profit. So Phase 1 comes down to one job: keep bad decisions away from that residual. Good people make bad calls in four ways. They decide on hope, so I use the outside view and write the reference-class figure beside my own. They are pushed by other people's interests, so I ask how everyone is paid and decide from today forward. They decide tired, so I keep a red window and check fitness. And they act on words that hid the risk or bound them by accident, so risk goes in the first line and structural changes are approved only in writing. The personal half matters too: a liquidity floor no deal can touch, concentration I have measured, and a will and powers of attorney before any guarantee.
terms: Control system — a set of written rules and checks that keeps a process within safe limits without relying on judgment in the moment.
Failure mode — a recurring way in which a decision or system goes wrong, such as deciding tired or on hope.
Investment committee — a group that must approve each major commitment of money against a written paper and an independent challenge.

hostile.q: You have a lot of rules for a developer who has not built anything yet. Why should a lender care?
hostile.a: Because a lender is lending against my decisions as much as against the building. My rules say how I decide: against written gate criteria, from a reference class, never in my worst hours, with risks stated first and every change confirmed in writing. And they say what I can survive: no deal is sized so its worst case breaches my liquidity floor. That is exactly the behaviour a lender is trying to judge.

title: The handshake that broke when the land got valuable
summary: A composite case: two friends develop a site on a handshake, one with land and one with work and cash. When the rezoning succeeds and the land quadruples in value, the partnership breaks, and every Phase 1 failure mode is visible in the wreckage. This lesson takes it through seven steps and ends with Rule 9.
rule: Rule 9: Before any partner puts in land, money or work, we sign a written agreement that fixes what each contributed and at what value, who decides, how gains are shared and how either of us leaves, including on death or incapacity; a handshake starts the negotiation, it never ends it.
body:
This is a composite example. No single real case is described, but every part of it is common. Two people trusted each other, agreed on a handshake, and were both honest. The deal still broke, because the land became valuable and nobody had written down what they had agreed when it was not.

Recall

Q. In Roman's Week 8 lesson, how do you size the cover a household needs?

A. Work backward from what the household would need to spend, and for how long, then subtract what existing assets and income would already provide.

Q. What is Rule 7?

A. Never let one project, or one lender's change of mind, be able to take everything; size every commitment so its worst case leaves your liquidity floor untouched.

Q. What is Rule 1?

A. No date, announcement or sunk cost moves me past a gate. Only the gate's written criteria do.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, your early deals are likely to involve people you know: a landowner who trusts you, a friend with capital, a relative with a site. Those are exactly the deals most likely to be done informally, and most likely to break when the stakes change. Ford chose this composite for the checkpoint because it uses every week of Phase 1: incentives, anchors, loss aversion, fatigue, communication, records, concentration and protection. Cole assists on the legal points. Everything legal here is conceptual and varies by jurisdiction; verify it with a lawyer.

Step 1: Timeline

Year 0. A landowner, call her the owner, holds a two-acre site her family has held for years, valued as farmland at about 500,000 dollars, a hypothetical figure. Her friend, a would-be developer, proposes they develop it together. Over dinner they agree: "Fifty-fifty. You bring the land, I bring the work and pay the costs." They shake hands.

Years 1 to 3. The developer spends about 300,000 dollars of his own savings on surveys, design and a rezoning application, and several hundred hours of his time. In year 3 the rezoning is approved. A broker values the site with its new permission at about 2,000,000 dollars.

Year 4. The owner's family, who were never part of the dinner, ask why half of a 2,000,000 dollar asset should go to someone who spent 300,000. The developer says the deal was fifty-fifty of the project. The owner falls ill and cannot make decisions for several months. A lender declines to fund the project because nobody can show who owns what or who can sign. The partnership ends in a dispute, and the approval lapses before the project starts.

Step 2: Key decisions

Three decisions mattered. Agreeing fifty-fifty without saying fifty-fifty of what: the land, the profit or the uplift. Spending 300,000 dollars, most of the developer's liquid savings, before anything was signed. And continuing to spend after the rezoning was filed, when the value at stake was visibly rising and the cost of disagreement was growing with it.

Step 3: Assumptions

Each assumed the other meant what they meant. The owner understood she was contributing land worth 500,000 dollars to a project and would receive half its profit. The developer understood that the land went into the deal at its value on the day of the handshake, so the rezoning uplift, his work, was shared. Both were reasonable readings of three words said at dinner. Both also assumed nothing would happen to either of them, so nobody thought about death or incapacity.

Step 4: Incentives

At year 0 the incentives were aligned: the owner had a field and the developer had a plan. The rezoning changed that. It created 1,500,000 dollars of value, and under one reading the owner received half of an uplift on her own land, while under the other she gave it away. The family's incentive was simple: they would inherit the land and not the partnership. Week 3's lesson applies exactly. People are not dishonest when their incentives move; they simply start to remember the agreement differently. Loss aversion did the rest. The owner now felt she was losing 750,000 dollars, not gaining a partner.

Say that out loud now.

Say it this way: the handshake was the same; the value changed, so the memory changed.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

There were several. The family asked questions in year 2 and were reassured over dinner rather than shown a document. The developer's own savings fell below any sensible liquidity floor, breaking Rule 7 in spirit, because the deal had become his single concentrated bet. A lawyer the developer consulted about the rezoning asked who owned the project vehicle and was told "we will sort that out." No confirming email after the dinner, no minutes of their meetings, and no record of the 300,000 dollars of spending were kept in a form anyone else could read.

Step 6: Point of no return

The point of no return was the rezoning approval. Before it, a fair written agreement was cheap: the land was worth 500,000 dollars and both sides could see a clear split. After it, every possible agreement made one side 750,000 dollars worse off than they believed they were entitled to, so no agreement could be reached without a dispute. The owner's illness then removed the one person who could negotiate for her side.

Step 7: Root cause

The root cause was a partnership with no written terms at the moment when terms were cheap to agree. Specifically, nothing fixed the value of the contributed land, what was being shared, who could decide, or what happened on death, incapacity or exit. Cole's audit view: there was no document anyone outside the two of them could rely on, which is why the lender walked away. Professional sign-off required: a lawyer, to draft any partnership or joint venture agreement, and a valuer for contributed land.

The prevention rule

Rule 9: Before any partner puts in land, money or work, we sign a written agreement that fixes what each contributed and at what value, who decides, how gains are shared and how either of us leaves, including on death or incapacity; a handshake starts the negotiation, it never ends it.

Worked example one, the arithmetic of the two readings. Reading A, profit-sharing on the whole: if the site sells for 2,000,000 dollars before construction, the developer first recovers his 300,000 dollars of costs and the remaining 1,700,000 dollars is shared equally, 850,000 each. The owner gets 850,000 and the developer 1,150,000. Reading B, land in at its day-0 value: the owner first receives her 500,000 dollars of land value, the developer recovers his 300,000 dollars of costs, and the remaining 1,200,000 dollars is shared, 600,000 each, so the owner gets 1,100,000 and the developer 900,000. The gap between readings is 250,000 dollars for each side. A one-page agreement at year 0 would have chosen one.

Worked example two, the cheap moment. At year 0, the same agreement would have taken one meeting and a modest legal fee. At year 4 it took a dispute, and the cost included a lapsed approval worth most of the 1,500,000 dollars of uplift. That is the cost of delay from Week 5, at its most extreme.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that the relationship makes the document feel insulting. The control is to frame it as protection for the relationship: "We agree now, while it is easy, so we never have to argue later."

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks trust replaces paper. Trust makes the paper easy to agree. It does not tell a lender, an heir or a court what you agreed.

Callback

In Week 6, Vera taught the confirming email: after any conversation that decides something, write it down within a day and invite correction. One numbered email after that dinner, "my understanding is: 1. land goes in at 500,000 dollars...", would have exposed the disagreement in year 0, when it cost nothing to fix.

Recap

A composite handshake deal broke when rezoning quadrupled the land value: the words had two readings, incentives moved, memories followed, one partner was over-concentrated and the other became incapacitated with no plan. Rule 9 puts the terms in writing before anyone contributes anything.

Next: Warrick, The Money, revisiting what delay, information and safety cost, with the Wealth Ledger.
checklist: Sign a written agreement before any partner contributes land, money or work.
Fix the value at which any land or asset is contributed, supported by a valuation.
State exactly what is shared: profit, uplift or the whole project.
Record who decides what, and how a deadlock is broken.
Cover death, incapacity and exit of each partner in the agreement.
Keep a ledger of every dollar and hour each partner contributes.
Confirm every partnership conversation that decides anything in writing within a day.
head: Field checklist
speak: This is a composite case, and a common one. Two friends agree on a handshake to develop a site fifty-fifty: one brings land worth about 500,000 dollars, the other brings the work and pays the costs. He spends 300,000 dollars of his own savings on design and a rezoning. When the rezoning is approved the land is worth about 2 million. Now fifty-fifty has two honest readings, and the gap between them is about 250,000 dollars a side. The owner's family push back, the owner falls ill with no power of attorney, the lender will not lend because nobody can show who owns what, and the approval lapses. The cheap moment to agree was the day of the handshake. My rule, Rule 9: before any partner puts in land, money or work, we sign a written agreement that fixes contributions and values, decisions, sharing and exit, including death and incapacity. A handshake starts the negotiation; it never ends it.
terms: Contributed land — land a partner puts into a joint project in place of cash, which must be given an agreed value at the time it goes in.
Uplift — the increase in a property's value created by an approval, a rezoning or development work.
Joint venture agreement — a written contract between partners in a project setting out contributions, control, sharing of gains and losses, and exit.

hostile.q: You and the landowner have known each other for years. Why do you need a lawyer-drafted agreement before you spend anything?
hostile.a: Because today the land is worth one figure and both of us agree on the split. If the rezoning succeeds, the value may multiply, and the same words can be read two ways. A one-page agreement now, while it is easy, protects our friendship and gives a lender something to rely on. It also covers what happens if either of us dies or cannot decide.

title: Checkpoint: the three prices every decision carries
summary: Phase 1 put a price on three things developers usually treat as free: time, information and safety. This checkpoint lesson revisits each with a worked example, joins them in one decision, and closes with the Wealth Ledger and a short thread on working with advisers.
body:
Mr Shabazz, every decision you make carries three prices whether you write them down or not: the price of time, the price of information and the price of safety. The developer who names all three, in dollars, decides better than the one who only sees the deal.

Recall

Q. What should you bring to a first meeting with an estate lawyer?

A. A current personal balance sheet, a list of how each asset is held, any guarantees and existing documents, and your questions, so the lawyer can advise on facts rather than guesses.

Q. What is the visible cost of a liquidity floor, and what is the hidden cost of not having one?

A. The visible cost is cash drag, the lower return on money held safe. The hidden cost of none is being forced to sell or borrow at the worst time.

Q. What is the developer's equity cheque?

A. The cash the developer and partners put in, usually before the lender advances, which is the first money at risk and the last repaid.

Why this matters

Phase 2 will teach the language of money in depth: net operating income, cap rates, cash flow and returns. Before it does, this checkpoint makes sure you carry three ideas from Phase 1 into every number you will meet. A pro forma shows profit. It does not show what you paid for waiting, what you paid to know, or what you paid to stay safe. Those are the prices that decide whether you are still in the business in ten years. All figures in this lesson are hypothetical and round.

The price of time

Plain English: once money is committed, every week costs interest and overhead whether or not anything happens. In Week 5, JAX priced a vague request: on a hypothetical 6,000,000 dollar loan at 8 percent, interest is about 9,230 dollars a week, and with 5,000 dollars of weekly overhead the carry is about 14,000 dollars. Two extra rounds of questions cost about 28,000 dollars.

The professional framing is cost of delay, and it applies to your decisions as much as anyone's. A slow yes costs carry. A slow no costs more, because you keep paying for a deal you will not do. The Phase 1 controls, bottom line first, the one-page memo and the confirming email, are delay controls.

The price of information

Plain English: a study is worth buying if the decision it might change is worth more than the study costs.

Worked example one. This is Roman's Week 1 example, extended with the price of time. A site shows a profit of 2,000,000 dollars if it is as it appears. You judge, in writing, a 25 percent chance of a hidden problem that would cost you 1,500,000 dollars if you bought. Without a study, expected value is 0.75 times 2,000,000, which is 1,500,000, minus 0.25 times 1,500,000, which is 375,000, giving 1,125,000 dollars.

Now a soil and zoning study costs 50,000 dollars and would reveal the problem if it exists, letting you walk away. With the study: 0.75 times 2,000,000 equals 1,500,000, minus the 50,000 study, equals 1,450,000 dollars. In the bad case you lose only the study. So the information is worth 1,450,000 minus 1,125,000, which is 325,000 dollars more than its cost.

Add time. The study takes 6 weeks, and holding the option costs a hypothetical 5,000 dollars a week, so 30,000 dollars. The study is still worth about 295,000 dollars more than it costs. Time and information priced together, on one page, in a form you can defend at a gate.

Say that out loud now.

Say it this way: what does it cost to wait, what does it cost to know, what does it cost to stay safe?

The price of safety

Plain English: safety costs a little every year and saves a lot in the year you need it.

Worked example two. Suppose you hold a liquidity floor of 150,000 dollars in cash earning about 3 percentage points less a year than you think you could earn in a deal. The cash drag is 150,000 times 0.03, which is 4,500 dollars a year. Now suppose, with no floor, a bad year forces you to sell a 400,000 dollar share of a project to a buyer who knows you must sell, at a 20 percent discount. That forced sale costs 80,000 dollars in one transaction. At those hypothetical figures, the floor costs about 4,500 dollars a year and one forced sale costs about eighteen years of it. The discount in a real forced sale may be larger or smaller; the point is that the cost of being forced is lumpy and arrives in exactly the year you can least afford it.

Insurance follows the same logic, from Week 8: you pay a known premium so a defined, larger loss falls on someone else, and you keep a reserve for the losses below the policy's retention.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

For your personal balance sheet, the three prices become three lines you review every quarter. First, liquid net worth against your floor: if the floor has been breached, no new commitment until it is restored. Second, contingent liabilities, above all personal guarantees, at their full possible amount, added to the worst case of every live deal; Rule 7 says that total must leave the floor untouched. Third, concentration: the share of your net worth that depends on one project or one market. A rising share is a decision you are making by default, and it deserves to be made on purpose. This is conceptual education, not financial advice; a licensed adviser is required before you act.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is pricing one of the three and ignoring the others, for example buying every study, so the deal dies of delay, or holding so much safety that you never invest. The control is to put all three on the same page of every gate memo: the cost of waiting, the cost of knowing and the effect on your floor.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats the expected value as a promise. It is an average over many decisions. A decision with a good average and a ruinous worst case is still a decision you do not take, which is why survivability sits beside expected value, not beneath it.

Working with advisers

Every one of these prices depends on advice: a geotechnical engineer on the chance of a problem, a lawyer on what a guarantee commits you to, a licensed financial adviser on your floor. Advice is an input you pay for, and it is only as good as the question you ask. Ask for the answer first, the range second and the reasons third, which is bottom line first applied to the people you hire.

Then do two things the best clients do. Ask how the adviser is paid and what their advice does to their pay, as you learned in Week 3. And write the advice into your decision journal with the date and the adviser's name, so that in a year you can see whose judgment held up.

Callback

In Week 2, Priya showed that optimism costs a project in delay and carry. The three prices are the antidote to optimism: an optimist assumes time is free, information is unnecessary and safety is wasted money. Naming each in dollars is how you replace a feeling with a number someone else can challenge.

Recap

Time costs carry, so decide and communicate clearly. Information is worth buying when the decision it may change is worth more than its cost, including the time it takes. Safety costs a little every year and saves a lot in the year you need it. Put all three on every gate memo, and review the Wealth Ledger every quarter.

Next: Omar, The Rules, revisiting the rules that already bind you: duty of care, your words and signature, guarantees and the documents that protect the base.
checklist: Write the weekly carrying cost of every live commitment.
Price every proposed study: chance it changes the decision, value of that change, cost and time.
Put the cost of waiting, the cost of knowing and the effect on your floor in every gate memo.
Review liquid net worth against your liquidity floor every quarter.
Add every personal guarantee at its full amount to the worst case of each deal.
Track the share of your net worth concentrated in one project or market.
Record each adviser's advice, with date and name, in your decision journal.
head: Field checklist
speak: Every decision carries three prices. Time: once money is committed, every week costs interest and overhead, so a vague request or a slow decision has a dollar cost I can calculate. Information: a study is worth buying when the decision it might change is worth more than it costs. On a hypothetical site with a 2 million dollar profit, a 25 percent chance of a 1.5 million dollar problem and a 50,000 dollar study, the study adds about 325,000 dollars of expected value, and still about 295,000 after six weeks of holding cost. Safety: a 150,000 dollar liquidity floor might cost 4,500 dollars a year in cash drag, while one forced sale at a 20 percent discount on a 400,000 dollar stake costs 80,000. So I put all three prices on every gate memo, and every quarter I check my liquid net worth against the floor, add every guarantee at full value, and measure my concentration.
terms: Cash drag — the return given up by holding money in cash or near-cash instead of investing it.
Forced sale — a sale made because the seller must raise cash by a deadline, usually at a discount to fair value.
Contingent liability — an obligation that becomes yours only if something happens, such as a lender calling a personal guarantee.

hostile.q: Why are you holding 150,000 dollars in cash when you could put it into this deal and earn far more?
hostile.a: Because that cash is my liquidity floor, and it is what stops a bad year from forcing me to sell a project stake at a discount. At these hypothetical figures it costs me about 4,500 dollars a year, and one forced sale could cost 80,000. I size every deal so its worst case, including any guarantee, leaves the floor untouched. That discipline is part of what you are relying on when you partner with me.

title: Checkpoint: the rules that already bind you
summary: Before Phase 3 teaches law properly, Phase 1 already introduced the legal ideas a developer meets every week: duty of care and the record of a decision, statements that become liability, words and signatures that bind, guarantees that reach your personal assets, and the documents that protect the base. This lesson revisits them as one map.
body:
Mr Shabazz, you are already bound by more rules than you have been taught. Phase 1 introduced them one week at a time; this lesson puts them on one map, so you can see where a single careless sentence, signature or missing document can reach past the project and into your own life.

Recall

Q. In the Auditor's Chair, how does Cole read a document?

A. As a hostile auditor would, assuming it will be relied on after something has gone wrong, and looking for anything that would not survive cross-examination.

Q. What four questions should you put to any personal guarantee?

A. How much is it capped at, what triggers it, when does it end, and must the lender pursue the company and the property before coming to you?

Q. Why should a land purchase usually wait for the land-use approval?

A. So the government's gate opens before your largest commitment rather than after it.

Why this matters

A developer's legal exposure does not begin when he signs a construction contract. It begins with the first conversation with a landowner, the first message to a lender and the first guarantee. Every one of the ideas below was taught as a concept, and every one varies by jurisdiction. That is the right way to hold them for now: as questions you know to ask, not answers you can rely on without advice. Verify each against the primary source and with a qualified lawyer before you rely on it.

Layer one: how you decide

Plain English: if you make decisions on behalf of others, such as partners, investors or a company, you are generally expected to decide with care and in good faith, and the best evidence that you did is a record made at the time.

The professional framing, from Week 2, is the duty of care owed by directors and others who manage on behalf of others, and in many places a business judgment principle under which courts are reluctant to second-guess an informed, good-faith decision that later turned out badly. What protects you is the process: what you knew, what you considered and why you chose. The decision journal, the one-page memo with its options and risks, and the minutes Vera taught in Week 6 are that process on paper. Note too the related principle from Week 4: in general, tiredness does not excuse a commitment, so the red window is a legal control as much as a physiological one.

Layer two: what you say and write

Plain English: words create liability in two directions. A false statement of fact can make you liable to someone who relied on it, and a reply that reads as agreement can bind you to terms you did not mean to accept.

The professional framing combines two Phase 1 lessons. From Week 3: puffery, vague sales talk such as "a wonderful location", is generally treated differently from a statement of fact, and a misrepresentation of fact that induces a contract can give the other side remedies even where the contract contains an entire-agreement clause, depending on its wording and the law. From Week 5: agreement is usually judged objectively, labels such as subject to contract can be overridden by conduct, and formal notices must follow the contract's notices clause.

Worked example one. A hypothetical marketing sheet for a small rental building says: "Fully leased. Guaranteed 8 percent yield." The building is 90 percent leased, and two leases end in three months. "Fully leased" is a statement of fact, and it is false. "Guaranteed" is a promise you may be unable to keep, made to people who may rely on it. A buyer or investor who relied on either line could have a claim. The Phase 1 rewrite: "90 percent leased as of 1 May; leases on 2 of 20 units end in July. Current net operating income supports a yield of about 7 percent on the asking price, before any change in occupancy." True, sourced and dated.

Say that out loud now.

Say it this way: facts I can prove, commitments I mean, notices by the clause.

Layer three: what reaches past the project

Plain English: a company with limited liability normally protects your personal assets from the project's debts. A personal guarantee deliberately removes that protection for the amount guaranteed.

The professional framing is from Week 7. A guarantee is a contingent liability: nothing today, the full amount on the day it is called. Where two or more people guarantee jointly and severally, the lender can usually pursue any one of them for the whole amount, leaving that person to recover a share from the others if they can. Ask the four questions in the Recall above before you sign anything.

Worked example two. Suppose, hypothetically, you and a partner jointly and severally guarantee a 1,000,000 dollar loan. You think of your exposure as 500,000 dollars. The loan defaults and your partner has no assets. The lender may pursue you for the full 1,000,000 dollars, and your claim against your partner may be worth nothing. On your Wealth Ledger, the guarantee belongs at 1,000,000 dollars, not 500,000, and Rule 7 asks whether your floor survives that number. Professional sign-off required: a lawyer qualified where the loan is governed, before you sign any guarantee.

Layer four: what happens when you cannot act

Plain English: if you die or lose capacity without the right documents, the law, not you, decides who controls your assets and who can sign for you, and that can freeze a project.

The professional framing is from Week 8. A valid will, meeting the formal requirements of the law that applies, names an executor and directs your estate. Powers of attorney, in many places capable of being made to continue through incapacity, let a person you choose act for you on property and on personal matters. Beneficiary designations on insurance and some accounts can pass those assets outside the will, which is why they must match your plan. Rule 8 sets the order: will and powers of attorney before your first personal guarantee. Professional sign-off required: an estate lawyer licensed where you live and where your assets are.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating these four layers as separate topics for separate professionals, so nobody sees that a guarantee signed in one office, a partnership agreed over dinner and an old beneficiary form in a drawer all point at the same personal balance sheet. The control is a one-page legal map of your own position, reviewed with your lawyer at every major deal: who decides, what you have said in writing, what you have guaranteed and what happens if you cannot act.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks legal risk starts with lawyers and contracts. Most of it is created earlier, in a quick reply, a brochure line, a handshake or a signature given to keep a deal moving, and the lawyer meets it only after it has become a problem.

Callback

In Week 1, REGA showed that the government holds its own gates: permits, inspections and the certificate of occupancy. Those are rules you cannot negotiate. The four layers in this lesson are different: they are rules whose effect on you depends on what you write, sign and record. That is why Phase 1 spent so much time on communication. Your words are where most of your legal position is made.

Recap

Layer one: decide with care and keep the record. Layer two: state facts you can prove and commit only to what you mean, with notices by the clause. Layer three: a guarantee reaches past limited liability, and joint and several means the whole amount. Layer four: a will and powers of attorney keep you in control when you cannot act. Everything here is conceptual; verify it with a lawyer where it applies.

Next: Roman, The Numbers, running one gate decision forward through every price and rule of Phase 1.
checklist: Draw a one-page legal map of your position: decisions, statements, guarantees, incapacity.
Keep a dated record of reasons for every decision you make for partners or investors.
Check every marketing or investor sheet line by line: is each statement a fact you can prove?
Replace guarantees of returns with sourced, dated current figures.
Record every personal guarantee at its full amount on your Wealth Ledger.
Put the four guarantee questions to any guarantee before you sign it.
Confirm your will, powers of attorney and beneficiary designations match before any new guarantee.
head: Field checklist
speak: I am already bound by more rules than I have been formally taught, and they sit in four layers. How I decide: if I decide for partners or investors, I am generally expected to act with care and in good faith, and my best protection is the record made at the time, the memo, the journal and the minutes. Tiredness is no excuse. What I say and write: a false statement of fact can create liability, puffery is treated differently, and a quick reply can bind me, so I state facts I can prove and commit only to what I mean. What reaches past the project: a personal guarantee removes limited liability for the amount guaranteed, and joint and several means the lender can usually pursue me for the whole amount. What happens when I cannot act: a will and powers of attorney, signed before any guarantee, keep a project from freezing. All of this varies by jurisdiction, so a lawyer confirms it.
terms: Duty of care — the obligation of a person managing on behalf of others to decide with reasonable care, skill and diligence.
Business judgment principle — the tendency of courts in many places not to second-guess an informed, good-faith business decision that turned out badly.
Joint and several liability — liability under which each of several people can be pursued for the whole amount, not only their share.

hostile.q: Your marketing sheet said fully leased. It is 90 percent leased. Why should we trust anything else in it?
hostile.a: You are right to challenge it; that line was wrong and I have withdrawn it. The corrected sheet states 90 percent leased as of the first of May, with two leases ending in July, and every figure on it now carries a date and a source. Our process is that no investor document leaves without a line-by-line fact check against the rent roll.

title: Checkpoint: one gate decision, run through every number in Phase 1
summary: This lesson runs a single hypothetical gate decision forward, step by step: from your own cost estimate to the reference-class adjustment, the profit test, the value of a study, and finally the test of your personal liquidity floor. It ends with the one-sentence bottom line you would put at the top of the gate memo.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a gate decision is not one number. It is a chain: your estimate, corrected by the outside view, tested against the margin you need, improved by information worth buying, and finally checked against what you personally can survive. Run the chain forward, in order, and the decision usually makes itself.

Recall

Q. What are the four failure modes from this week's First Principles lesson?

A. Deciding on hope, being pushed by other people's interests, deciding tired or stressed, and acting on words that hid a risk or bound you by accident.

Q. What does the concentration ratio measure?

A. The share of your net worth that depends on a single asset, project or market.

Q. What is expected value?

A. The average outcome of a decision, found by multiplying each possible outcome by its probability and adding the results.

Why this matters

Each Phase 1 week gave you one calculation. A lender, a partner or your own investment committee will want them together, in a defined order, so they can see that the deal clears every test and not just the flattering one. All figures below are hypothetical and round. Thresholds such as a required margin or a guarantee cap are commercial choices, not standards.

The deal at the gate

You hold an option on a site and must decide by month's end whether to buy. Your inputs: land 1,500,000 dollars; your own estimate of construction cost, called hard cost, 8,000,000 dollars; soft and finance costs, meaning fees, permits, interest and similar, 1,800,000 dollars; completed value 14,000,000 dollars, from a market study. Your partners require at least 15 percent profit on cost.

Steps 1 and 2: your estimate, then the outside view

Step 1, inside view. Total cost: 1,500,000 plus 8,000,000 plus 1,800,000 equals 11,300,000 dollars. Profit: 14,000,000 minus 11,300,000 equals 2,700,000 dollars. Profit on cost: 2,700,000 divided by 11,300,000, about 24 percent. It looks comfortable.

Step 2, outside view, Rule 2. Suppose your reference class, the actual outcomes of similar projects you have gathered, shows hard costs finishing a median 15 percent above early estimates. That figure is hypothetical for this exercise; your own reference class must come from real data. Adjusted hard cost: 8,000,000 times 1.15 equals 9,200,000 dollars. Adjusted total: 1,500,000 plus 9,200,000 plus 1,800,000 equals 12,500,000 dollars. Profit: 1,500,000 dollars. Profit on cost: 1,500,000 divided by 12,500,000, which is 12 percent.

Write the two figures side by side, as Rule 2 requires, and explain any reason you believe your project will beat the reference class. If you cannot name one, the 12 percent is your planning figure.

Step 3: the margin test, run backward

The partners need 15 percent. The most the project can cost and still deliver it: 14,000,000 divided by 1.15, which is about 12,170,000 dollars. The adjusted cost of 12,500,000 is about 330,000 dollars too high. So the deal fails the gate as it stands, unless you can find about 330,000 dollars of savings, evidence for a higher value, or a lower land price. That last one matters: you hold an option, so a renegotiated land price is a real lever.

Say that out loud now.

Say it this way: 24 percent on hope, 12 on the reference class, and 330,000 short of the line.

Step 4: the price of information

Suppose a geotechnical study costing 40,000 dollars would tell you whether the soil needs deep foundations. You judge a 20 percent chance that it does, adding 1,000,000 dollars of cost. Without the study, the expected foundation cost is 0.20 times 1,000,000, which is 200,000 dollars, a cost you cannot price into your offer with confidence. With the study, you either confirm normal footings or you learn the extra cost before you buy and negotiate the land price down by it, or walk away. The study converts a 20 percent chance of a 1,000,000 dollar surprise into a known number before your largest commitment, for 40,000 dollars. Buy it, and make the purchase conditional on its result.

Run the bad branch too. If the study shows deep foundations are needed, the adjusted total cost rises from 12,500,000 to 13,500,000 dollars, against a value of 14,000,000, leaving 500,000 dollars of profit, under 4 percent on cost. No land price the seller is likely to accept rescues that, so you let the option lapse. You have spent 40,000 dollars to avoid a commitment that would have put about 1,000,000 dollars of extra cost on a project with no margin to carry it. That is the price of a gate, from Week 1, paid in the right currency.

Now a revised offer. If the study comes back clean and you negotiate the land down by 350,000 dollars to 1,150,000, the adjusted total becomes 12,150,000 dollars, profit 1,850,000 dollars and profit on cost about 15.2 percent. The deal clears the gate, just.

Step 5: the personal test, Rule 7

The project's numbers are not the last test. Your own balance sheet is. Suppose, hypothetically, equity is 30 percent of cost, about 3,650,000 dollars, of which your share is 10 percent, about 365,000 dollars. The lender asks for your personal guarantee, capped at 500,000 dollars. Your liquid assets are 900,000 dollars and your liquidity floor is 150,000 dollars.

Worst case: your equity is lost and the guarantee is called in full. 365,000 plus 500,000 equals 865,000 dollars. 900,000 minus 865,000 leaves 35,000 dollars, far below your 150,000 dollar floor. Rule 7 fails. The deal may clear the project gate and still be one you must not sign as structured.

Fix the structure, not the rule. Negotiate the guarantee cap down to 300,000 dollars. Worst case: 365,000 plus 300,000 equals 665,000 dollars. 900,000 minus 665,000 leaves 235,000 dollars, above the floor. Now the deal passes both gates. If the lender will not reduce the cap, a partner might share the guarantee, or you take a smaller share.

Step 6: the bottom line

Put the result at the top of the gate memo, in the order you learned in Week 6. "Recommendation: proceed only on three conditions: a clean geotechnical study, the land price reduced to 1,150,000 dollars, and my personal guarantee capped at 300,000 dollars. On reference-class costs the project then delivers about 15 percent on cost; on my own estimate it delivers about 24 percent, which I am not relying on." One sentence of recommendation, three conditions, two numbers and an honest statement of which one you trust.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is stopping the chain early, usually at Step 1, because the inside-view answer is the one you want. The control is the order itself: no gate memo is complete until all six steps are on the page, including the personal test.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats the personal test as private and separate from the deal. It is part of the deal. A lender is relying on your survival as well as the building's, and a structure that would breach your floor is a risk to every party, not just to you. A sponsor forced to sell his other assets in a crisis is distracted at exactly the moment the project needs him most.

Callback

In Week 6, Nadia showed that a number in a memo hides an assumption. This chain is the remedy at scale: every number in the final recommendation can be traced back to a stated input, the reference-class adjustment, the study, the negotiated land price and the guarantee cap, so nobody has to reverse engineer it to find out what you assumed.

Recap

Run a gate forward in six steps: inside view, outside view, margin test, price of information, personal test, bottom line. Here the inside view said 24 percent, the reference class said 12, the margin test showed a 330,000 dollar gap, a 40,000 dollar study and a land renegotiation closed it, and a lower guarantee cap made it survivable. All figures are hypothetical.

Next: Kema, The Room, running a full mock gate meeting with a lender, a partner and a contractor.
checklist: Write the inside-view cost, value and profit on cost for every gate decision.
Adjust hard cost by your reference-class figure and write both results side by side.
Work back from the required margin to the maximum total cost the project can bear.
Price every study that could change the decision, and make the purchase conditional on it.
Use land price, guarantee cap and share size as levers before abandoning a deal.
Run the Rule 7 worst case: lost equity plus full guarantee against liquid assets and floor.
Put a one-sentence recommendation with its conditions at the top of the gate memo.
head: Field checklist
speak: I run a gate decision forward in six steps. First, the inside view: on hypothetical numbers, land 1.5 million, hard cost 8 million, soft costs 1.8 million and value 14 million give about 24 percent on cost. Second, the outside view: if similar projects overran hard cost by 15 percent, cost becomes 12.5 million and the margin falls to 12 percent. Third, the margin test: to deliver 15 percent, the project can cost at most about 12.17 million, so I am about 330,000 short. Fourth, information: a 40,000 dollar soil study turns a 20 percent chance of a million-dollar surprise into a known number before I buy, and a clean result plus a lower land price clears the line. Fifth, the personal test: lost equity plus the full guarantee must leave my liquidity floor intact, so I negotiate the cap down. Sixth, the bottom line, with conditions, at the top of the memo.
terms: Inside view — an estimate built from the details of your own project, before comparison with similar past projects.
Hard cost — the direct cost of construction: labour, materials and equipment for the building and site works.
Soft cost — the indirect costs of development, such as design fees, permits, legal and finance costs.

hostile.q: Your own estimate shows 24 percent. Why are you presenting 15 to us?
hostile.a: Because 24 percent is my inside view, and similar projects have historically overrun early hard-cost estimates. On the reference-class figure the project delivers about 12 percent as offered, which fails our 15 percent threshold, so I am recommending we proceed only with a clean soil study, a land price of 1,150,000 dollars and my guarantee capped at 300,000. If my estimate proves right, the upside is yours as well, but I will not ask you to rely on it.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Checkpoint: the full mock gate meeting
summary: A full mock meeting at the gate decision from yesterday's lesson, with a lender, an equity partner and a contractor at the table. Each exchange tests one Phase 1 skill: bottom line first, numbers aloud, the hostile question, Rule 6, the holding answer, listening and silence, and the confirming email that closes it.
body:
Mr Shabazz, this is the meeting Phase 1 has been preparing you for. Read it once straight through, then read it again and say your lines aloud before you read them, as though the people were in the room.

Recall

Q. What is Rule 9?

A. Before any partner puts in land, money or work, we sign a written agreement that fixes what each contributed and at what value, who decides, how gains are shared and how either of us leaves, including on death or incapacity; a handshake starts the negotiation, it never ends it.

Q. In the guarantee meeting, what does a lender really want to know when it asks what you are worth?

A. Whether you could support the project, and would still be standing and engaged, if it went wrong, which is a question about liquidity and concentration, not headline net worth.

Q. Who sits at a gate meeting besides you?

A. Typically the lender, equity partners, the design and cost team and the contractor, each with their own interest in the decision.

Why this matters

Knowing the controls is not the same as using them with three people watching and a clock running. This mock meeting compresses Phase 1 into thirty minutes. Each exchange tests one skill. If you can run it calmly in rehearsal, you can run it in a real room, because the real room will ask very similar questions.

Before the meeting

You set the meeting for 14:00 on a day off, not the morning after a night shift: the red window, Rule 4. You sent the one-page gate memo yesterday. You have a number sheet with every figure, its unit, its period and its source. You have written down the three most hostile questions you expect and drafted an answer to each. You have taken one slow breath, seated, before walking in.

Exchange 1: the opening

Say: "Thank you for coming. The bottom line: I recommend we proceed with the purchase on three conditions, a clean soil study, the land price reduced to 1,150,000 dollars and my personal guarantee capped at 300,000 dollars. On those terms the project delivers about 15 percent on cost using reference-class costs. I'll take you through the three conditions, then your questions."

Never say: "So, a bit of background first." The answer goes first.

Exchange 2: the lender and the numbers

The lender asks: "What's your total cost?"

Say: "About 12.2 million dollars, using reference-class hard costs 15 percent above our own estimate. Our own estimate gives about 11 million, but I'm not relying on it." One number per sentence, with the unit and a comparison. Then stop.

The lender follows up: "And the soft costs include interest at what rate?" You do not have the exact rate assumption on your sheet.

Say: "I don't have the rate assumption in front of me. I'll confirm it in writing by Friday, with the interest calculation." Never say: "About 7 percent, I think." A guess spoken in a meeting becomes the figure in the lender's notes.

Exchange 3: the partner's hostile question

The partner leans in: "Your own estimate said 24 percent a month ago. Now it's 15. Why should we trust either number?"

Breathe once. Acknowledge: "That's fair. The 24 percent was my inside view." Bridge: "The question that matters is which figure we should plan on." Answer: "The 15 percent, because it uses what similar projects actually cost, not what I hoped. And it only holds with the land price and the soil study as conditions. If the study fails, I'm recommending we walk away." Then stop talking.

Listen for the question behind the question. The partner may really be asking whether you will keep moving the number. If so, add a control the partner can check: "From now on you'll get a one-page cost report on the first of every month, so you see any movement as soon as I do."

Say that out loud now.

Say it this way: that's fair; the question that matters is; here is the answer; then silence.

Exchange 4: the contractor's verbal change

The contractor, keen to show savings, says: "We could save about 150,000 dollars by switching the parking deck to a lighter slab. The engineer said on site it sounded fine."

This is Rule 6 in a live room. Say: "That's welcome, and I'd like to pursue it. Please submit it as a written substitution request. It's a structural change, so it needs the engineer of record's written approval with calculations before we count the saving." Never say: "Great, let's go with that." You would be agreeing a structural change and counting an unconfirmed saving in front of a lender.

Exchange 5: the lender on the guarantee

The lender says: "We normally ask for a guarantee of 500,000 on a loan this size."

This is a negotiation, so listen first. Ask: "What is the guarantee there to protect against, completion or cost overrun?" Then be silent and let them answer fully. If the answer is completion risk, you can offer what addresses it: "I understand. My limit is 300,000 dollars, because my own balance sheet has to survive the worst case. I can offer a larger contingency and monthly cost reporting to reduce the completion risk you're concerned about." Never say: "That's fine," to a number you have not tested against Rule 7.

Exchange 6: the close

Say: "Let me confirm where we are. One, the partners will decide by Friday on proceeding on the three conditions. Two, I'll send the interest rate assumption by Friday. Three, the contractor submits the slab change as a written substitution request. Four, the lender will come back on the guarantee cap by next Wednesday. I'll circulate these as minutes today."

Then send the confirming email that afternoon, numbered, dated, with a request to correct anything by a stated date, as Vera taught in Week 6. That evening, run a short after-action review in your decision journal: what you expected the meeting to decide, what it actually decided, why any difference arose and what you will prepare differently next time. Note how many hours you had slept, too. Over a year, those entries become your own reference class for how meetings go.

Holding your state

If the room turns cold, keep both feet on the floor, slow your speech a notch, and treat the jolt as readiness. If you feel yourself about to fill a silence, count two seconds first. The person who stays calm usually ends up running the meeting. These are practitioner habits drawn from stress research; check any persistent symptoms with your doctor.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that one strong personality turns a gate decision into a conversation, and the meeting ends warmly with nothing decided. The control is the close in Exchange 6: every meeting ends with numbered, owned, dated actions, read aloud and then sent in writing.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner tries to win every exchange. The goal is not to win. It is to leave with a sound decision, every figure accurate, no accidental commitment, and the trust of all three parties intact. Conceding a fair point is often what wins the room.

Callback

In Week 5 you sat at a landowner's kitchen table and learned to ask, summarise, check and only then offer. Exchange 5 is the same skill under more pressure: you asked what the guarantee protects against before offering anything, which let you trade a control the lender valued for a cap you could survive.

Recap

Prepare: the right hour, the memo, the number sheet and your three worst questions. Open with the bottom line. Say numbers with units and comparisons, and confirm by Friday when you do not know. Acknowledge, bridge and answer, then stop. Hold Rule 6 against verbal changes. Listen before trading. Close with numbered, owned, dated actions, and send them in writing.

Next: Kema, the Phase 1 Checkpoint, with a mock interview, your recorded three-minute explanation and the rules you will not break.
checklist: Schedule any gate meeting outside your red window.
Send the one-page memo a day ahead and bring a number sheet with units, periods and sources.
Write and rehearse answers to your three most hostile questions.
Open with the bottom line and the conditions in the first two sentences.
Answer any figure you do not have with a dated written confirmation.
Require written substitution requests for any change raised verbally in the meeting.
Close by reading back numbered, owned, dated actions, then send them as minutes that day.
head: Field checklist
speak: A gate meeting tests every Phase 1 skill at once. I schedule it outside my red window, send the one-page memo a day ahead and bring a number sheet. I open with the bottom line: proceed on three conditions, about 15 percent on cost using reference-class figures. When the lender asks for a number I have, I say it once, with its unit and a comparison. When I do not have it, I say I'll confirm it in writing by Friday. When a partner challenges me, I acknowledge what is true, bridge to what matters, answer and stop. When the contractor offers a structural saving based on a remark from the engineer, I ask for a written substitution request under Rule 6. When the lender asks for a bigger guarantee, I ask what it protects against before offering anything, and I hold to what my balance sheet can survive. I close with numbered, owned, dated actions and send them in writing that afternoon.
terms: Gate meeting — the meeting at a planned decision point where the next commitment of money is approved or refused against written criteria.
Number sheet — a one-page list of the figures you may be asked for, each with its unit, period and source.
Read-back — restating the agreed actions aloud at the end of a meeting so everyone hears the same list before it is written down.

hostile.q: We normally take a 500,000 dollar guarantee on a loan this size. Why should we accept 300,000?
hostile.a: Because my balance sheet has to survive the worst case, and at 500,000 it would not, which should matter to you as much as to me. If your concern is completion and cost overrun, I can offer a larger contingency in the budget and a monthly cost report to your monitor. I would rather give you controls that reduce the risk than a guarantee that could leave me unable to see the project through.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Phase 1 checkpoint: the mock interview and the three-minute recording
summary: The Phase 1 checkpoint. A mock interview with a lender and an investor across every subject of the phase, model answers to compare against, the instruction to record a three-minute explanation on your phone and score it for accuracy, structure, composure and the hard question, and the rules you have written so far, to read aloud and restate.
body:
Mr Shabazz, this is the end of Phase 1. Today you are not reading; you are performing. Answer an interviewer aloud, record yourself explaining the phase in three minutes, score it honestly, and then read every rule you have written so far and put each one in your own words.

Recall

Q. What are the three prices every decision carries?

A. The price of time, the price of information and the price of safety.

Q. In the Week 7 review, what makes a personal financial summary misleading to a lender?

A. Typically assets at hoped-for rather than current selling values, missing contingent liabilities such as guarantees, and no distinction between liquid and illiquid assets.

Q. What is a developer's profit, and why is it fragile?

A. It is the residual left after every other party is paid, so a small change in value or cost becomes a large change in profit.

Why this matters

A checkpoint is retrieval under pressure. Research on learning consistently finds that recalling something from memory strengthens it more than rereading it, and that doing so in conditions like the real ones, out loud, with a clock and a hard question, prepares you for those conditions. The people who will judge you as a developer, lenders, partners and officials, will not ask whether you have read about judgment or communication. They will watch whether you use them. This is your first rehearsal.

Part one: the mock interview

Imagine a lender's credit officer and an experienced private investor across the table. Answer each question aloud before reading the model answer. Keep each answer under a minute.

Interview question 1. "What do you actually do as a developer?"

Model answer: "I control the few things that decide the residual, value, cost, time, risk and financing, and I decide at planned gates, against written criteria, whether to commit the next block of money."

Interview question 2. "How do you know your cost estimate is any good?"

Model answer: "I don't trust my own estimate alone. I put the reference-class figure beside it, what similar projects actually cost, and I plan on that unless I can explain in writing why mine will do better."

Interview question 3. "You work rotating shifts. Why should I trust decisions you make at 4 in the morning?"

Model answer: "You shouldn't, and I don't make them. I keep a written red window: no signatures, payments or new commitments overnight or straight after a night shift. Urgent items get a holding reply and an answer by a stated time."

Interview question 4. "Your last update said things were on track. Then there was an overrun. Why?"

Model answer: "That's fair, and the update put reassurance above the risk, which was wrong. My rule now is that any open risk goes in the first line with what it would take to close it. You will see that in every report."

Interview question 5. "What happens to this project if you're hit by a bus?"

Model answer: "I have a will and enduring powers of attorney, signed before any guarantee, and my partnership agreement covers death and incapacity. The project has someone with authority to sign the next day."

Interview question 6, the hard one. "If this deal goes wrong, can you survive it?"

Model answer: "Yes, by design. My worst case, lost equity plus the full guarantee, still leaves my liquidity floor untouched. If a structure breached it, I would change the structure or not do the deal."

Say that out loud now.

Say your own answer to question 6 again, slower, and stop when you have answered.

Part two: the three-minute recording

Open the voice recorder on your phone. Set a timer for three minutes. Explain Phase 1 to an imagined lender who has never met you: what a developer does, how you decide, how you protect decisions from your own biases and fatigue, how you communicate, and how you protect your balance sheet and your family's position. Do not read notes. Then play it back once and score yourself from 1 to 5 on each line below.

MeasureWhat a 5 sounds like
AccuracyEvery concept and number is right; nothing is overstated, and laws are described as concepts to verify.
StructureThe bottom line comes in the first sentence, followed by about three supporting points.
ComposureEven pace, real pauses, no filler, and no rush at the end.
The hard questionYou named the weakest point yourself and answered it with a control.

Write the four scores and the date in your decision journal. Any score of 3 or below: reread that week's First Principles lesson and record again in three days. Keep the recording. You will record again at every checkpoint, and the difference between the first and the fifth will tell you more than any grade.

Part three: the rules you will not break

Below this lesson are the rules you have written so far, one from each week's Failure Forensics. Read each rule below aloud, then restate it in your own words. If your restatement changes the meaning, read the rule again. A rule you cannot say in your own words is a rule you will not use when it is inconvenient, which is exactly when you need it.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is skipping the recording because it is uncomfortable to hear yourself. The discomfort is the point: it shows you what a lender hears. The control is to do it now, before anything else today, and to put the next recording date in your calendar.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner scores himself generously and moves on. Score as a sceptical credit officer would. A half-remembered rule counts as a miss, because in a real meeting a half-remembered rule turns into a guess.

Callback

In Week 2 you learned the after-action review: what was supposed to happen, what happened, why the difference, what next. Run one on your recording. What did you plan to say, what did you actually say, why the gap, and what will you change in three days? The recording is the most honest after-action review you will get this year.

Recap

Phase 1 taught one system that protects a thin residual: gates, the outside view, incentives, fatigue rules, clear communication, written records, a liquidity floor, and the documents that protect the base. Today you used it aloud in an interview, recorded and scored yourself on accuracy, structure, composure and the hard question, and restated your rules in your own words.

checklist: RULES_SO_FAR
head: Rules I will not break
speak: Phase 1 taught me one system. A developer is paid last, from a thin residual, so my job is to keep bad decisions away from it. I decide at gates, against criteria written in advance. I put the reference-class figure beside my own estimate. I ask how every adviser is paid, and I decide from today forward, not from sunk cost. I keep a red window, so I never sign, pay or commit when I am exhausted. I communicate bottom line first, with any risk in the first line and every number said with its unit and period. I confirm what was agreed in writing within a day, and I approve structural changes only in writing with the calculation. I never guess; I confirm by Friday. And I protect the base: a liquidity floor no deal can touch, every guarantee counted at full value, and a will and powers of attorney signed before my first guarantee.
terms: Checkpoint — a planned review at the end of a phase that tests whether you can use what you learned under realistic conditions.
Retrieval under pressure — recalling knowledge aloud, against a clock and a hard question, to prepare for using it in real meetings.
Self-scoring rubric — a short set of measures and descriptions of a top score, used to judge your own performance consistently.

hostile.q: If this deal goes wrong, can you survive it?
hostile.a: Yes, by design. I size every commitment so that its worst case, my equity lost and any personal guarantee called in full, still leaves my liquidity floor untouched. If a structure would breach that floor, I change the structure, by lowering the guarantee cap, sharing it or taking a smaller share, or I do not do the deal.
